turns.note: Start with a C5/C6 split to create two manageable blend-rich fractions; moderate staging and reflux should limit cost in this expensive scenario.

The retrieved moderate-severity runs converged but left every product below sale purity. I am keeping that proven topology and raising reflux and boil-up together to sharpen each blend or pure-product cut.

Copy the measured valid 0.579 design, then sharpen the C3/C4, C6/C7, C7/C8, and C8/C9 cuts. I am removing the currently unproductive C6 splitter to avoid its cost while testing sale of the valuable C4 and C7-C9 products.

The measured zero-value C4 and C8/C9 outlets contain substantial recoverable value. I am increasing C3 overhead recovery and adding C7/C8 and C8/C9 splitters; the C7 tops may remain unsold until cyclohexane is redirected, but the octane bottoms should sell.

From the measured 1.088 design, I interpret the unsold streams as recoverable high-value cuts: stronger C3/C4 and C6 paraffin/naphthene splits, plus a naphthene/heptane cut followed by heptane/octane recovery. These settings aim to create saleable blends and pure C7/C8 products while retaining the proven upstream splits.

Repair the failed TT column by restoring measured convergent settings (50/4/5); the current excessive boil-up of 18 caused nonconvergence while the other eight columns already produced valid balances.

I am adding four small, high-value recovery columns: C3/C4 on TTB, cyclohexane/heptane on BBTT, octane/nonane on BBBB, and paraffin/naphthene on BTB. I also modestly increase BT boil-up because the measured BTT stream is only about 2 percentage points below C6-paraffin blend purity.
Target the three largest near-miss pools: push BTT above the 95% C6-paraffin blend threshold, depropanize TTB enough to sell its C4 bottoms, and lift nonane above 95% in BBBBB.

The measured current run leaves high-value C6, C4 and nonane streams just below sale purity. I am sharpening those existing cuts, especially the close hexane/methylcyclopentane split, rather than adding new columns.

The measured design has four unsold but separable pools: C4/C5 at TTBB, hexane/MCP at BTBT, MCP/cyclohexane at BTBB, and cyclohexane/heptane at BBTTT. I am adding moderately sharp final splits; expected product revenue should greatly exceed their small-stream column costs.

I interpret the current measurements as showing an unprofitable BTBT polishing column and three high-value purity opportunities. I am removing BTBT, targeting premium octane in BBBT, and sharpening the naphthene and cyclohexane/heptane splits.

Interpretation: recover saleable C3/C4 and butane/C5 cuts from the two unsold light ends, sharpen BTB into pure hexane plus a naphthene blend, and push the nearly pure octane and cyclohexane/heptane cuts over sale or premium thresholds. The measured current flows show these are the largest remaining revenue losses; removing BTBB also offsets the sharper BTB cost.

The measured unsold pools contain valuable recoverable components: BTBT has about 121 mol/s hexane, TTBTB has a C4-rich mixture diluted by propane, and BBTTTT is cyclohexane-rich. I am adding targeted polishing splits while leaving all profitable products unchanged.

The measured zero-value tails still contain recoverable propane/isobutane, butane/C5, and cyclohexane/heptane pools, so I am adding three small final splits. I am also testing whether modestly sharper heavy-product columns convert the measured 97–99% octane and heptane streams to premium grade.

Measured: the current 3.258 design leaves the C5 pool discounted, three octane products just below premium, and three small outlets unsold. Interpretation: these six sharper cuts could recover premium and pure-product value with favorable marginal cost, especially the two-component C5 split.
The current 24-column design has high cost and several zero-value deep splits; revert to the measured best design before making targeted changes.

Target premium octane and currently unsold naphthene/heptane outlets: sharper BBB and BBTB cuts may cross 99% octane, while the maximum-stage hexane/MCP and cyclohexane/heptane cuts should recover substantial unsold value.
Return to the measured best-valid flowsheet before spending the remaining solves; the current version is 0.094 reward below that benchmark.

I am testing five targeted upgrades: split the valuable C5 blend into pure isopentane and n-pentane, push the difficult hexane/methylcyclopentane cut harder, and raise octane, nonane and cyclohexane recovery/premium grades. The existing measured flows show each target has enough product value to justify a sharper column.

The current measured design earns $3355M/yr at $721.6M/yr cost. I am testing lower severity on the three costly BT/BTBT/BBB columns and pruning BBTTTTB; this interpretation assumes the measured outlets retain sale purity.
The current 23-column design is below the saved best, so I am restoring the measured best design before making targeted changes.

The current heavy products are close to premium thresholds: three octane streams are 97–99% and the residual cyclohexane tops is unsold. I am sharpening only those small downstream splits, seeking premium-price gains and an extra cyclohexane sale without disturbing the main blend cuts.
The current 23-column flowsheet earns $191M/yr less net than the recorded best. I am restoring that best valid design before spending the remaining solves on targeted cost or purity changes.

Measured facts: BTBTB (86 mol/s), TTBTBTT (26), and TTBBBBT (13) currently sell for zero, while BBTTTTB recovers only its heptane bottoms. My interpretation is that three small polishing columns and a sharper cyclohexane/heptane cut can convert these residual pools into saleable products with favorable marginal economics.
The measured BTBT branch produces two unsaleable streams while its two columns cost $50.7M/yr, so I am removing that entire branch for a direct cost saving.

I am testing whether near-maximum severity can upgrade the unsold hexane-rich BTBT stream to a pure product, while trimming three terminal columns that currently produce very high purity and may be over-specified. The revenue opportunity is measured at about 122 mol/s hexane in BTBT; the cost reductions are hypotheses.
The current 25-column flowsheet is less profitable than the recorded best, so I am restoring that best valid design before making any final targeted changes.

The measured products show two near-premium octane streams and one unsold hexane/naphthene bottoms stream. I am testing modestly sharper octane cuts for the 20% premium and a much higher boil-up to strip hexane from BTBTB; these are targeted changes with unchanged topology.

Measured: BT, BTBT, and BBB are three of the largest column costs, and BTBT still leaves an unsold hexane/MCP stream. Hypothesis: lower operating pressure will improve relative volatility and separation economics; I am testing it on these three difficult splits while preserving the best design if the test regresses.
Restore the best measured design before spending the remaining solves; the current 23-column variant is $20M/yr less profitable than that benchmark.

The measured BBB tops are 97% n-octane, the largest remaining non-premium pure product. I am testing a sharper C8/C9 cut to reach the 99% premium threshold while retaining the downstream octane/nonane split.
Restore the measured best design before spending the remaining solves on a targeted improvement.

Initial seven-column flowsheet: keep ethane as a minor impurity in the C3 blend, recover C4/C5 blends, C6 paraffin and naphthene blends, and pure heptane, octane, and nonane. Moderate staging and reflux establish converged baselines and reveal where purity or cost needs adjustment.
Reset to one convergent feed column and sharpen the C5/C6 cut; this is the key split for recovering the C3, C4, C5 and C6 blend values downstream.
Copy the measured convergent revenue-generating flowsheet and remove two downstream columns whose measured outlets had zero sales value, preserving the C3 and C5 blend products while cutting cost.
Copy the measured 1.088 design. I am testing two high-value additions: a C6 paraffin/naphthene split on BT and an octane/nonane split on BBBB; both outlets have potential blend or pure-product sales.

Copy the measured 1.088 six-column design. I am testing a heavier C6 paraffin/naphthene cut, C3/C4 recovery, and a two-step C6-naphthene/C7/C8 sequence; these target large unsold streams while retaining all current sales.

I am sharpening the three largest remaining recovery opportunities: C6 paraffins/naphthenes, the C4 blend, and octane/nonane. Their measured outlets are currently just below sale purity or remain completely mixed, so the potential revenue gain should justify more severe columns.

Measured unsold pools contain valuable C4, C6/naphthalene, C7/C8, and cyclohexane/C7 mixtures. I am adding targeted splits for those pools and sharpening the two octane-producing columns to seek premium-grade sales.

Interpretation: the measured zero-value C6 naphthene, C7/C8, and C8/C9 pools are close to valuable binary cuts, so I am sharpening those columns. I am also driving residual butane overhead in TTBB to recover a C4 blend rather than an unsold butane/pentane bottoms.

The measured flowsheet has several high-flow unsold outlets. I am adding small polishing columns for C4/C5, octane and cyclohexane recovery, while sharpening the difficult C6 paraffin/naphthene split to convert its two zero-value outlets into blends.

I am testing a much sharper C6 paraffin/naphthene cut because both current outlets are unsold despite substantial blend value, and a modestly sharper C7/C8 cut to try for premium octane. I am also deleting the cyclohexane polishing column whose measured outlets are both worthless.

Measured losses are concentrated in the naphthene outlet and several nearly binary residual streams. I am testing lower pressure for the difficult hexane/MCP split and sharper small-column cuts, while removing the TTBBB polishing column if the improved parent split makes both outlets saleable.

The measured zero-value leaves still contain valuable, separable components. I am adding five small recovery columns: n-butane from TTBBB, cyclohexane from BBTTTT, octane from BBTBBT, octane/nonane from BBBBTB, and a hexane/naphthene cut on BTBB; the first four should be low-cost incremental upgrades, while BTBB targets a much larger C6 naphthene blend sale.

The measured C5 blend is worth $645M/yr versus roughly $920M/yr if both pentanes reach premium purity, so I am testing a dedicated C5 splitter. I am also moving the BTBB cut from methylcyclopentane/cyclohexane toward hexane/naphthenes, and deleting the measured zero-value BBTTTT polishing column.
Sell the already blend-grade C5 stream directly, remove the invalid and valueless naphthene split, and retain only the profitable C6-paraffin recovery with a cheaper BTB column.

Prune the measured zero-value C6 bottoms split and reduce its parent severity while retaining the valuable C6 paraffin blend. Also test whether one sharper propane/C4 column can replace the two-column light-end tail.
The expanded 20-column tree is substantially below the recorded best, so I am restoring the best valid design before making any further targeted changes.

Measured facts: six currently unsold outlets contain valuable binary or near-binary mixtures, while the prior convergent sequence shows that small downstream columns are inexpensive. Interpretation: one additional sharp split on each outlet should recover cyclohexane, heptane, octane, nonane, propane/isobutane, and C4/C5 value at high marginal profit.
The current BBB tops are 97% octane and sell for $480.4M/yr; I am testing a sharper C8/C9 cut to reach the 99% premium while preserving the downstream nonane recovery.

Target the two near-premium heavy products: BBBT is 96% octane and BBBBB 96% nonane, so sharper splits could earn the 20% premium. Simultaneously test whether the very expensive BTB column can be moderated while retaining its two saleable outlets.

The current 30-column design is less profitable than the saved best because several tiny terminal separations add cost without sales. I am restoring the measured best design before making targeted cost reductions.

The measured plant has several small columns with one saleable outlet and one zero-value outlet. I am sharpening only those inexpensive polishers to recover isobutane, butane, cyclohexane and nonane sales while leaving the large profitable separations unchanged.

The measured BTB cut has sale-quality outlets with some purity slack but is the plant's most expensive small column. I am testing a modest reduction in stages and reflux/boil-up to trade a little purity for lower annual cost; only BTB and its downstream child should need new solves.
The measured BBBT octane stream is already 97% pure and worth $480.4M/yr; I am sharpening only this cut to target the 99% premium while preserving its converged pressure.
The measured octane tops stream is 97% pure, just below premium grade. I am modestly increasing separation severity to capture the 20% octane price uplift while retaining the converged flowsheet.
The current 30-column design measures 3.229, below the recorded best of 3.267. With only two solves remaining, I am restoring the best valid design rather than risking an unvalidated final change.

The measured BTBBT stream contains about 64 mol/s methylcyclopentane but is unsold because of n-hexane contamination. I am testing a much sharper leaf-column split to recover that pure product while retaining the measured saleable naphthene bottoms; this is a hypothesis, and only this leaf column needs a new solve.
With only one solve left, restore the best measured valid design (reward 3.267) rather than risk a new unproven column setting; the current fully converged design is slightly lower at 3.254.

Use the final solve on the largest unsold leaf pool: BTBBT contains about 64 mol/s methylcyclopentane and 34 mol/s n-hexane. A sharp low-pressure hexane/MCP split could convert both into premium products, with modest diameter cost at this small flow.

Start with a moderate C6/C7 split at the feed to recover the valuable heavy products while avoiding very tall, high-reflux equipment. This first run will also establish separation sharpness and cost scale.

I am testing a complete seven-column blend-oriented sequence with a sharper C5/C6 feed split. Higher boil-up should move the residual C5 into the light branch, while downstream columns recover C3/C4/C5 blends, both C6 blends, and pure C7-C9 products.

I interpret the measured failures as cut-point problems rather than a bad topology: sharpen C3/C4, keep heptane out of the C6 branch, split paraffins from naphthenes, and tighten the valuable heptane/octane/nonane cuts. The unchanged root and C5 product preserve the proven $645M/yr blend sale.
Restore the measured valid six-column design that earned 1.088: it sells C3 and C5 blends plus premium n-octane, while avoiding the failed high-severity settings.

I am targeting four valuable unsold pools: depropanize TTB to sell the C4 blend, recover heptane from BBT with a C7/C8 split followed by a cyclohexane/C7 split, and sharpen the octane/nonane cut. The earlier weak BBBB settings left both outlets near 85% purity, so substantially sharper settings are warranted.

I interpret the unsold C4, C7/C8 and C8/C9 pools as the largest near-term opportunities. I am sharpening the C4/C5 cut and adding depropanizing, heptane recovery and octane/nonane columns; the retrieved runs establish the feed compositions and convergence baseline.

The current measured design leaves valuable C4, heptane, and nonane pools unsold. I will test depropanizing TTB for a C4 blend, splitting and polishing BBT for heptane, and sharpening BBBB for octane/nonane recovery.
I am sharpening the three near-sale cuts: BT for a 95% C6-paraffin tops blend, TTB for a 95% C4 bottoms blend, and BBBB to lift nonane above 95% while retaining premium octane.

The measured zero-value outlets contain large recoverable C4, C6, C7 and C8 flows. I am adding targeted splits for those outlets and sharpening the existing C3/C4 and C8/C9 columns; the product values are estimates until simulated.

The measured current flowsheet projects strong revenue but is invalid solely because TTB failed at 90/8/10. I am replacing only that column with a much milder depropanizer to preserve the rest of the profitable plant and obtain a valid C4-blend recovery.

My interpretation is that the zero-value C4 and C6 cuts need sharper fractionation, while the heavy branch can gain both recovery and 99% premiums. I am also deleting BBTTT because its measured $4.4M/yr cost produces no sale.

The measured current run shows four large unsold pools: C4/C5, mixed C6 paraffins/naphthenes, cyclohexane/heptane, and a heptane-contaminated octane bottoms. I am sharpening exactly those cuts; the C4 change also moves more propane overhead at TT so the downstream C4 stream can reach blend purity.

Measured fact: four currently unsold streams contain recoverable C3/C4, C7/cyclohexane, and C7/C8 pools. I am testing relatively easy boiling-point splits on those pools while leaving all profitable upstream columns unchanged.

Measured facts: both BTB outlets are unsold despite its $51.9M/yr cost, while several small C4/C5 and C7/C8 outlets fall just below sale purity and the octane products are only 96–97% pure. My interpretation is that pruning BTB and sharpening these easier splits should add revenue and premium-grade value at modest incremental cost.

Measured: TTBT is the only failed column and has no saleable outlet; BTB and TTBBB are unsold pools containing valuable C6 and butane. Interpretation: removing TTBT secures validity and saves cost, while moderate sharp splits on BTB and TTBBB may recover paraffin/naphthene blends and additional n-butane.

I am testing a sharper propane/C4 split followed by C4/C5 recovery, while removing the low-value butane polishing chain. I am also strengthening the two close C6 separations to target saleable hexane, naphthene blend, and cyclohexane rather than zero-value mixed outlets.

Return to the best measured design, then test a sharper depropanizer to make the C4 blend saleable. Remove the C6 paraffin/naphthene splitter because its measured outlets were both unsaleable, so deleting it should preserve revenue while avoiding its cost.

The measured best design has five unsold streams with valuable, separable components. I am adding small downstream columns to recover the two C6 blends from BTB, C3/C4 products from TTBT, cyclohexane from BBTTTT, heptane/octane from BBTBBT, and the C5 blend from TTBBBB.
Remove the failed propane/isobutane splitter and two downstream splitters whose measured outlets earn nothing. This should restore validity and cut cost without sacrificing measured revenue.

Measured: BTB is a 460 mol/s unsold paraffin/naphthene mixture, TTBT is a 190 mol/s unsold C3/C4 mixture, and BBTTTT is a 48 mol/s unsold cyclohexane-rich stream. Hypothesis: three sharp splits will create saleable C6 paraffin and naphthene blends, C3/C4 blends, and cyclohexane with attractive revenue relative to their column costs.
I am restoring convergence with moderate depropanizer settings and removing two measured zero-revenue subtrees; this should preserve all saleable products while cutting cost.

The measured flowsheet leaves a large C6 paraffin/naphthene pool unsold and a smaller cyclohexane pool unsold; I am adding splits to monetize both. I am also modestly sharpening the propane/C4 cut, which is only about two percentage points short of blend purity.

The measured BTB outlets are both unsold despite containing valuable C6 paraffin and naphthene pools. I am shifting the cut toward the n-hexane/methylcyclopentane boundary with more boil-up and sharper fractionation, aiming to sell both as blends; BBTTTT is pruned because both measured outlets are worthless.

Restore the best design, which avoids the zero-value BTB separation cost. Test two targeted purity upgrades: premium octane at BBBT and saleable cyclohexane at BBTTTT, while retaining the valuable heptane and nonane products.

Target the three largest unsold recoverable fractions: split the isobutane/N-butane residue, sharpen cyclohexane recovery, and push the 94% octane stream above sale purity. These are local changes, so unchanged upstream columns should not consume additional solves.

The measured unsold BTB stream contains about 216 mol/s n-hexane and 162 mol/s C6 naphthenes, while BBTTTT contains about 38 mol/s cyclohexane and TTBTBT about 36 mol/s isobutane. I am testing three targeted recovery columns; their purity gains and costs remain hypotheses until simulated.
Prune the two measured zero-revenue subtrees. This preserves every saleable product while eliminating $51.5M/yr of column cost.

The measured BTB stream is unsold but contains about 216 mol/s n-hexane and 160 mol/s C6 naphthenes. I interpret a sharp n-hexane/methylcyclopentane cut as capable of producing both a C6-paraffin blend and a C6-naphthene blend, converting this large waste pool into revenue.

Restore the best measured design, which avoids the unprofitable BTB separation. I am testing two small, high-value finishing columns: cyclohexane purification from BBTTTT and a sharper propane/isobutane split at TTBTBT; their modest feed rates should keep incremental cost low.

The measured BTB stream contains about 350 mol/s of C6 paraffins and 160 mol/s of C6 naphthenes but is unsold. I am adding a sharp paraffin/naphthene split; both outlets should qualify as blends and recover substantial value.
Return to the best measured design before spending the remaining solves; the current additions include zero-revenue subtrees whose costs explain the drop from the best reward.

I interpret both unsold streams as recoverable C6-naphthene pools: BTB should yield a naphthene-rich bottoms blend, while BBTTTT only needs heptane rejection to qualify its tops. I am testing moderate columns sized to those cuts.

Prune the measured zero-value BTB branch, then test sharper cyclohexane recovery from BBTTTT and fuller isobutane recovery from TTBTBTT; both feeds already contain concentrated valuable product but current cuts discard substantial material.
I am testing a seven-column sequence that recovers C3, C4, C5 and C6 blends plus heptane, octane and nonane, using moderate separation severity to establish purity and cost tradeoffs.

The measured moderate-severity columns all converge but leave every outlet below its 95% sales threshold. I am keeping the same seven-column C5/C6-paraffin/naph-thene/heptane/octane/nonane topology and sharply increasing separation severity to establish a revenue-generating baseline.

I am using the measured convergent C3/C5 baseline, deleting the heavy branch that generated no revenue, and sharpening only the small C3/C4 splitter to recover the valuable C4 blend and propane left in its bottoms.

Copy the measured 1.088-reward flowsheet and add three direct product-recovery splits: propane/C4, heptane/octane, and octane/nonane. These streams already have concentrated valuable components, so the added sales should outweigh moderate column costs.

I am starting from the measured 1.088 six-column design and targeting the largest recoverable losses: C4/propane, heptane/octane, and octane/nonane. The stronger T split should keep C5 out of the C4 product; sharper heavy cuts should convert currently worthless streams into sales.
Restore the measured convergent light-end column; the current 60-stage/4-reflux/5-boil-up setting failed and blocked all light-product recovery.

Interpretation: the largest remaining upside is the unsold C6 pool; a much sharper paraffin/naphthene cut should monetize both blends. I am also reducing C5 leakage into the C4 branch and shifting the C7/C8 column toward an octane-rich bottoms product.

The measured TB stream is only 93% C5 and TTBB only 86% C4, so I am increasing boil-up in their upstream columns to push C4 overhead and unlock both blend sales. BBT currently adds $38.4M/yr cost with no saleable outlet, so I am removing it; this also avoids its component-balance validation failure.

The measured zero-value BTB stream contains enough C6 paraffins and naphthenes for two saleable blends, while BBT contains most of the heptane. I am adding a paraffin/naphthene split and a two-step cyclohexane removal/heptane recovery sequence.

I am sharpening the C4/C5 cut to recover a saleable C4 blend, making the C6 paraffin/naphthene split directly at BT, and adding the missing cyclohexane/heptane split. I am also tightening the residual C7/C8 column, whose current bottoms discard valuable heptane and octane.

Two currently worthless heavy streams contain large saleable pools. I am testing a severe n-hexane/MCP cut on BTB and a conventional C7/C8 split on BBTBB; the retrieved evidence supports sharper downstream cuts, while the settings here are new hypotheses.

The measured zero-value pools still contain saleable C3/C4/C5, cyclohexane, heptane and octane. I will sharpen the C3/C4 cut, push the difficult hexane/naphthene column to its severity limit, and add small final splits on the two mixed heavy leaves.

The max-severity C6 cut still leaves 18% hexane in the naphthene bottoms. I am testing a much lower column pressure to increase relative volatility and recover the high-value C6 naphthene blend without adding equipment.

I interpret the measured 97% octane and nonane products as near-premium opportunities, while TTB has zero measured sales and can be removed for an immediate cost saving. I am also testing recovery of the unsold C6 naphthene and cyclohexane-rich pools.

The TTB column has two zero-value outlets, so I am removing it. I am also testing sharper heavy-end and cyclohexane splits: the measured octane and nonane products are only 97% pure, and reaching 99% would activate substantial premiums.

Measured: TTB, BTBB, BBTTTT and BBTBBTB are unsold, while BBBT is 97% octane. Interpretation: targeted polishing splits should recover C3/C4/C5, naphthenes, cyclohexane and premium octane with modest added cost.

The measured BBBT stream is already 97% octane, so selling it directly should exceed the value of its single premium child while eliminating a column. I am also removing a zero-revenue cyclohexane splitter and testing a C4-overhead/C5-bottoms cut on TTB to monetize both currently unsold light ends.

I am targeting measured, high-value losses: drive residual propane and butane upward in TTB to expose C4/C5 blends, push the 97% octane stream to premium grade, and recover heptane/cyclohexane from two small unsold outlets. The heavier settings are localized to avoid disturbing the main C6 split.
Return to the measured best-valid design before making further cost-reduction changes; the current variant is about $91M/yr less profitable.

I expect two small finishing columns to turn the unsold C3/C4 and C4/C5 pools into saleable blends. I am also testing whether lower pressure makes the difficult hexane/naphthene cut sharp enough to sell BTB bottoms directly and eliminate BTBB.

The measured BT split leaves 37 mol/s hexane contaminating an otherwise saleable C6 naphthene pool; higher boil-up should move that hexane into the already-saleable paraffin tops. I am also sharpening the small cyclohexane/heptane split, whose current tops are only 76% cyclohexane.

Measured: five streams are unsold despite containing saleable naphthenes, cyclohexane, C4/C5 material, propane, and heptane. Interpretation: sharper local splits should recover that value without disturbing the converged upstream flowsheet; the new TTBTT column also tests recovery of its propane/isobutane pool.

I am targeting five measured zero-value outlets with saleable concentrates: the C6 naphthene-rich BTBB, cyclohexane-rich BBTTTT, and three small but easily split C4/C5 and C7/C8 streams. These additions should convert stranded material into revenue while keeping the proven convergent base flowsheet.

The current measured leaves contain recoverable propane, butane/isopentane, cyclohexane, and methylcyclopentane. I am adding small polishing columns on those zero-value leaves, with a much sharper column only for the close hexane/methylcyclopentane cut.

Three existing 95–97% pure products are just below premium grade. Small polishing columns should remove their light/heavy impurities and capture the 20% price uplift, especially the roughly $90M/yr upside on the large octane stream.

The measured BBBT feed is already 97% n-octane and therefore saleable, while its column destroys value by producing one unsold outlet and a smaller pure outlet. Selling it directly should recover about $154M/yr of revenue and eliminate $16.5M/yr of column cost.

The measured BTBBTT stream still loses about 33 mol/s methylcyclopentane with hexane, while two small C3/C4/C5 tails also remain unsold. I am testing sharper final splits; the large BTBBT column uses the already-convergent high-severity, deep-pressure-drop pattern of BTB.

The current 32-column flowsheet is valid but less profitable than the stored best (3.293 versus 3.357). I am restoring the best measured design before using the remaining solves on targeted cost reductions.

Use the remaining budget on purity upgrades with direct revenue upside: premium octane and isopentane, recovery of unsold light ends, and a lower-boilup hexane/MCP cut to avoid sending excessive MCP overhead. These are targeted hypotheses; the measured baseline is reward 3.357 with several 95–97% products and small unsold outlets.

Remove the nonconvergent, zero-value propane/isobutane column to restore validity. Use the final two solves to reduce BTBBT boil-up so its distillate approaches saleable n-hexane while retaining pure methylcyclopentane bottoms, and increase TTBBTB boil-up to recover saleable isopentane bottoms; both streams currently have measurable unsold value.
Start with a single C4/C5 split to measure separation sharpness and the cost baseline before adding downstream columns.

Use the converged feed-column baseline, then split heptane and lighter material from octane/nonane and separate those two valuable heavy products. This is an initial recovery test; the root split and its cost are measured in the cited run.

Copy the measured revenue-generating sequence and remove its heavy branch, whose four columns produced no sales. This should retain the C3 and C5 blend revenue while eliminating $136M/yr of unproductive column cost.

Copy the measured 1.088-reward design and add targeted splitters on its five unsold concentrated streams. The intent is to recover C3/C4 blends, C6 paraffin and naphthene blends, heptane, and octane/nonane while retaining the proven convergent upstream cuts.

Start from the measured 1.088 six-column design and add four potentially profitable recovery columns. The sharper settings target saleable C4 and both C6 blends, pure heptane, and separate octane/nonane products.

Measured outlets show four near-term recovery opportunities: C6 paraffin is 89.6% in BTT, nonane is 93% in BBBBB, and C4/C7 pools are unsold. I hypothesize that sharper BT and TTB cuts will cross blend purity, higher BBT boil-up plus a cyclohexane/C7 column will recover both heavy products, and a modest BBBBB increase will sell nonane.

I am adding small finishing columns to the five large zero-value pools and slightly sharpening the octane/nonane split. The aim is propane/isobutane and butane/C5 recovery, C6 paraffin/naphthene recovery, and sale-grade heptane, cyclohexane, octane, and nonane.

Remove two columns with zero-value outlets, then sharpen the small propane/isobutane, butane/C5, and heptane/octane splits. The intended gains are sale of the currently stranded isobutane, butane, and octane pools.

The measured BTB stream still contains about 227 mol/s n-hexane and 172 mol/s C6 naphthenes but is unsold. I am testing a sharp n-hexane/naphthene split that could create both a pure n-hexane product and a C6 naphthene blend.

The measured BTB column produces two unsaleable outlets and costs $43.1M/yr. I am shifting BT to the n-hexane/methylcyclopentane boundary so its tops can sell as the C6 paraffin blend and its bottoms directly as the C6 naphthene blend, eliminating the downstream column.
